title: Sol, the Unconquered Sun
summary: A month with Sol, the Roman sun: the old Sol Indiges of the Quirinal, the sun of the Circus and the obelisks, Aurelian’s Sol Invictus and the birthday of 25 December, Horace’s prayer for Rome, and a practice of greeting the dawn.
welcome:
This journey runs about a lunar month and begins, most days, at sunrise. You will learn who Sol was to the Romans, from the old god of the Quirinal hill to the Unconquered Sun of the later empire, how he was pictured and prayed to, what is known and argued about his midwinter birthday, and how people honour him today. There is a nine-dawn practice of greeting the sun, and at the end you may make a self-dedication.

It is a self-dedication, not an initiation. Aurelian founded a college of pontiffs for Sol, and the mysteries of Mithras, who was also called Sol Invictus, had their own grades of initiation; nothing here revives either. What anyone can do is what many Romans did: greet the rising sun, give him incense and light, and keep his days.

If you can, begin about a month before the winter solstice, so that the dedication falls on 25 December, or before the summer solstice. Never look directly at the sun.
about: Sol is the sun, honoured as a god. Romans counted him among their oldest gods: Varro lists Sol among the gods the Sabine king Titus Tatius brought to Rome, and an old shrine of Sol Indiges stood on the Quirinal hill, with a festival on 9 August. He shared a temple with Luna, the moon, at the Circus Maximus, where the chariot races were said to be held in his honour, and Augustus dedicated to him the two great Egyptian obelisks he brought to Rome. Poets pictured him driving a four-horse chariot across the sky, and Latin literature took over the Greek myths of Helios. In AD 274 the emperor Aurelian, after his victories in the East, built Sol a magnificent new temple, gave him a college of pontiffs and games every four years, and made Sol Invictus, the Unconquered Sun, one of the chief gods of the empire. A calendar of AD 354 marks 25 December as the birthday of the Unconquered, with thirty chariot races. Sunday, dies Solis, is still his day by name. Today Roman polytheists honour Sol at midwinter and at dawn, and many modern Pagans greet the returning sun at Yule.
notes: Never look directly at the sun, even at sunrise or sunset, and never through binoculars, a camera or a telescope. Face the sunrise with your eyes lowered or closed, or look at its light on the land.

You will often read that Christmas was placed on 25 December to replace Sol Invictus’s birthday. That is one scholarly view. Others argue the Christian date came from calculating the Annunciation, and some doubt that the pagan festival is older than the Christian one. The journey sets out the debate.
Sol Invictus was also a title of other sun gods: Elagabal of Emesa, whom the emperor Elagabalus imposed on Rome, and Mithras in the mysteries. The journey says which is which.

Sun symbols are old and everywhere, but a few modern ones, such as the so-called “black sun”, are used by extremist groups and have nothing to do with Roman religion. The gods of Rome belong to anyone who approaches them with respect, whatever their ancestry.

stages.title: Facing east
stages.intro: Before study, a greeting at sunrise. Sol is the most visible of the gods; you have seen him every day of your life. This short rite in the Roman form introduces you to him as the light comes up, with incense and a lamp, and asks for nothing.

practices.title: Find the sunrise
practices.instructions: On each of the two days, find out the time of sunrise where you live and where on the horizon the sun comes up. Look for a window, balcony, garden or street corner that faces east. Watch the light change for five minutes, with your eyes on the sky and the land, never on the sun itself.
practices.prompt: Where does the sun rise for me? What did the light do as it came?

rite.title: Greeting Sol
rite.summary: A short Roman-form greeting at sunrise: washed hands, covered head, Janus first, then incense and a lamp for Sol, a raised right hand, and Vesta last.

ingredients.name: A bowl of clean water and a towel
A scarf or fold of cloth to cover your head
An incense burner or a heatproof dish with sand
An oil lamp or gold candle in a stable holder
A little honey on a small dish

rite.preparation: The evening before, set out the burner, the lamp and the dish by an east-facing window or door. Check the time of sunrise and set an alarm a quarter of an hour before. Read the words through until you can say them without stumbling.

steps.title: Wash and veil
steps.instructions: Before the sun rises, wash your hands and face and dry them. Draw the cloth over the back of your head, as a Roman did to pray.

steps.title: Janus first
steps.instructions: Light the lamp. Drop a few grains of incense on the burner. Janus, god of doors and beginnings, is called first in Roman prayer, and the dawn is the door of the day.
steps.spoken:
Father Janus, opener of the way,
opener of the day,
receive this incense, and carry my words through.

steps.title: Greet Sol
steps.instructions: As the light comes, face east with your eyes lowered. Raise your right hand, palm outward, the gesture with which Sol himself is shown greeting the world. Add incense.
steps.spoken:
Sol, bright and life-giving,
who bring out the day in your shining chariot and hide it again,
or by whatever name you rightly wish to be called:
I greet you at your rising.
I come to learn who you are.
Be honoured by this incense and this light.

steps.title: Honey
steps.instructions: If you have honey, set the dish before the lamp.
steps.spoken: Sol, be honoured by this honey. I ask nothing this morning but to be known to you.

steps.title: Stand in the light
steps.instructions: Stand for a few minutes as the light grows, eyes on the brightening sky or the land, never on the sun. Feel the warmth, if there is any.

steps.title: Vesta last, and turn
steps.instructions: Name Vesta last, as Roman prayer ended with her. Turn round to your right, uncover your head and put out the lamp.
steps.spoken: Vesta, keeper of the hearth, be honoured, last as always.

rite.closing: Leave the honey until evening, then put it out for the earth or the compost. Write down the date and the time of sunrise: you have begun.
rite.safety: Never look directly at the sun. Never leave a lamp, candle or incense unattended, especially if you go back to bed. Keep incense smoke away from birds and anyone with asthma. Keep honey from babies under a year old.

stages.title: The sun of Rome
stages.intro: Five lessons, about two days each. They go from the old Sol of the Quirinal, to his place at the Circus and on the obelisks, to Aurelian’s Unconquered Sun, to how he is honoured today, and finally to the hard parts: the Christmas debate, the sun of emperors, and Phaethon’s fall.

lessons.title: Who Sol is
lessons.summary: The sun as a god, Sol Indiges of the Quirinal, his image, and his companion Luna.

sections.heading: The sun as a god
sections.body:
Sol is the sun, and the Romans did not separate the god from the light. His name is simply the Latin word for the sun, as Luna is the word for the moon. That makes him unusual among Roman gods, most of whom have names that are not ordinary words. He is the god you can see.

Varro, the great antiquarian of the first century BC, names Sol among the gods to whom the Sabine king Titus Tatius vowed altars in early Rome, along with Luna, Saturn, Flora and others (On the Latin Language 5.74). Whether or not the story is true, it shows that Romans thought of Sol as one of their oldest gods, not a foreign arrival.

sections.heading: Sol Indiges
sections.body:
An old shrine of Sol Indiges stood on the Quirinal hill. Indiges is an old and puzzling word, often taken to mean “native” or “of this land”. The surviving calendars mark a sacrifice to Sol Indiges on the Quirinal on 9 August. Quintilian mentions a pulvinar, a sacred couch, of the Sun near the temple of Quirinus.

Very little is known about how Sol Indiges was worshipped. He seems to have been a modest, steady presence in the Roman calendar for centuries, not one of the great gods of the state. That changed only in the third century AD.

sections.heading: His image
sections.body:
Romans pictured Sol as a young, beardless man with a crown of rays around his head, driving a four-horse chariot, a quadriga, across the sky. In many images he raises his right hand, palm out, in a gesture of greeting or blessing; sometimes he holds a globe or a whip. The rays and the chariot came to him with the Greek Helios, and the image was everywhere in the Roman world: on coins, mosaics, gems and lamps.

His animals are the horses of his chariot. Later writers give them names. His plants, for modern devotees, are the bay laurel he shares with Apollo and golden flowers; his colours gold, yellow and white.

sections.heading: Sol and Luna
sections.body:
Sol is often paired with Luna, the moon. They shared a temple at the Circus Maximus and appear together on monuments, often at the top corners of a scene, Sol on one side and Luna on the other, framing the world between day and night. Horace’s Secular Hymn, sung in 17 BC, calls on both.

Later, Romans also identified Sol with Apollo, as the Greeks had come to identify Apollo with Helios. That identification is mostly literary and philosophical. In cult, Apollo and Sol kept separate temples and festivals.

knowAndDont.known: Varro (On the Latin Language 5.74) lists Sol among Titus Tatius’ gods. The calendars mark Sol Indiges on the Quirinal on 9 August. His radiate, chariot-driving image is attested on thousands of objects. The temple of Sol and Luna at the Circus is mentioned by Tacitus (Annals 15.74) and others.
knowAndDont.unknown: What Indiges meant, and what rites were given to Sol Indiges, are unknown. The Titus Tatius story is legend. How far ordinary Romans in the Republic prayed to Sol at all is unclear.

lessons.inPractice: Learn the times of sunrise and sunset this month, and say a word to Sol at one of them each day, even from a bus or a kitchen window.
reflect: What is it like to meet a god you can see every day?
What does the light of the sun make possible in your life that you never think about?
further: Steven E. Hijmans, Sol: The Sun in the Art and Religions of Rome (2009)
Varro, On the Latin Language 5.74 (Kent’s 1938 Loeb translation on archive.org)

lessons.title: The Circus, the obelisks and the dawn
lessons.summary: Why the chariot races belonged to Sol, the obelisks Augustus gave him, Horace’s prayer, and soldiers greeting the sunrise.

sections.heading: The chariot races
sections.body:
The Circus Maximus, the great racecourse of Rome, had a temple of Sol at its side, and ancient writers linked the races themselves with the sun. The Christian writer Tertullian, attacking the games around AD 200, says the circus is chiefly consecrated to the Sun, whose temple stands in its middle and whose image shines from its top (On the Spectacles 8). Later writers explained the whole circus as a picture of the year: twelve starting gates for the months, seven laps for the days of the week or the planets, four colours of the racing factions for the four seasons, and the four-horse chariot for the sun.

Those explanations are learned and late, but they show how naturally Romans connected the chariot race with the sun’s chariot across the sky.

sections.heading: The obelisks
sections.body:
After he conquered Egypt, Augustus brought two great obelisks from Heliopolis, the Egyptian “city of the sun”, to Rome in 10 BC. One stood on the central barrier of the Circus Maximus; the other became the pointer of a vast sundial on the Campus Martius. Both bases carried the same inscription: Augustus, “Egypt having been brought under the power of the Roman people, gave this as a gift to Sol”.

Both still stand in Rome, in the Piazza del Popolo and the Piazza di Montecitorio. They are among the few things in the city you can still touch that were dedicated to Sol.

sections.heading: Horace’s prayer
sections.body:
In 17 BC Augustus held the Secular Games, a great festival for the start of a new age, and Horace wrote the hymn sung by a choir of boys and girls. It contains a prayer to Sol that is one of the loveliest in Latin: “Life-giving Sun, who with your shining chariot bring out the day and hide it, and are born another and the same, may you never see anything greater than the city of Rome” (Secular Hymn 9–12).

“Born another and the same”: each sunrise is a new sun and the same sun. That idea is at the heart of honouring Sol, and it is why his birthday later fell at the turning of the year.

sections.heading: Greeting the dawn
sections.body:
Did Romans greet the sunrise? Tacitus tells of a night battle in AD 69 near Cremona. At dawn the soldiers of the Third Legion, who had served in Syria, hailed the rising sun, “as is the custom in Syria”, and their opponents thought they were greeting reinforcements (Histories 3.24–25). The detail shows that greeting the sun at dawn was known, and that Tacitus thought of it as an eastern custom.

Greeks did it too; Plato describes Socrates standing all night and then praying to the sun at sunrise. Modern Roman polytheists and many Pagans have made it a daily practice, and it is the simplest devotion to Sol there is.

knowAndDont.known: Tertullian (On the Spectacles 8) links the circus to the Sun. The obelisk inscriptions (CIL VI 701 and 702) survive and record the gift to Sol. Horace’s Secular Hymn and its date are certain. Tacitus, Histories 3.24–25, describes the legion greeting the sun.
knowAndDont.unknown: How old the link between the races and Sol really is, as opposed to later learned explanation, is debated. How widely ordinary Romans greeted the dawn is unknown; Tacitus presents it as Syrian.

lessons.inPractice: Learn Horace’s prayer, in Latin or English, and say it at sunrise: “Alme Sol, curru nitido diem qui promis et celas aliusque et idem nasceris…” Use it as your morning greeting for the rest of the journey.
reflect: “Born another and the same.” What in you is new each morning, and what stays the same?
What would it mean to greet each day as the soldiers did, before the work began?
further: Horace, Secular Hymn (Carmen Saeculare) (public-domain translations on Project Gutenberg)
Tacitus, Histories 3.24–25 (public-domain translations on Project Gutenberg)

lessons.title: Aurelian and the Unconquered Sun
lessons.summary: The temple of AD 274, the pontiffs and games of Sol, the birthday of 25 December, and the other suns called Invictus.

sections.heading: Aurelian’s temple
sections.body:
In the troubled third century, the empire nearly broke apart. The emperor Aurelian (ruled 270–275) pulled it back together, defeating the breakaway kingdom of Palmyra in the East in 272. Back in Rome, in 274, he built a splendid temple to Sol, filled it with treasure from his victories, and founded a new college of pontiffs, the pontifices Solis, ranked alongside Rome’s ancient priesthoods. He also founded games for Sol, held every four years.

Sol Invictus, the Unconquered Sun, became one of the chief gods of the empire. Coins of Aurelian call Sol “lord of the Roman empire”. For about fifty years, until the reign of Constantine, the radiate sun god was everywhere on imperial coinage.

sections.heading: Roman or Syrian?
sections.body:
Scholars used to say Aurelian brought in a Syrian sun god, perhaps the god of Emesa or the sun of Palmyra, and gave him a Roman name. That view is now strongly challenged. The historian Steven Hijmans and others argue that Aurelian’s Sol was the old Roman Sol raised to new honour, with Roman priests and a Roman temple, and that the eastern-sun theory rests on a misreading of the sources.

The question matters because two other gods were also called Sol Invictus. The emperor Elagabalus (ruled 218–222), himself a priest of the sun god Elagabal of Emesa in Syria, brought that god’s sacred black stone to Rome and tried to place him above Jupiter; after Elagabalus was murdered the stone was sent home. And Mithras, the god of a popular mystery cult among soldiers and officials, was also called Sol Invictus in inscriptions. These were different gods with a shared title.

sections.heading: The birthday of the Unconquered
sections.body:
A Roman calendar made in AD 354, the Chronography of Filocalus, marks 25 December as N(atalis) Invicti, the birthday of the Unconquered, with thirty chariot races. In the old Roman reckoning, 25 December was the winter solstice, the day the sun stops sinking and begins to return. The same document, in its list of Christian feasts, also records the birth of Christ on 25 December.

That is the earliest firm evidence for the festival. Whether Aurelian himself founded a festival on that day, as is often said, is not recorded; his games for Sol seem to have been held in October. The festival of the Unconquered may be older than 354, or it may not.

sections.heading: Sunday
sections.body:
The seven-day planetary week, with each day named for a planet, spread through the Roman world in the first centuries AD. The first day was dies Solis, the Sun’s day, still Sunday in English and Sonntag in German. In 321 the emperor Constantine ordered that courts and city workshops rest on “the venerable day of the Sun” (Codex Justinianus 3.12.2), while letting farmers work if the weather required.

Constantine’s coins carried Sol until the 320s. How he himself understood the sun and the Christian God is one of the great debated questions of late Roman history.

knowAndDont.known: Aurelian’s temple, pontiffs and games are recorded in the Historia Augusta, Zosimus and inscriptions naming pontifices Solis. The Chronography of 354 marks N Invicti on 25 December. Constantine’s law of 321 survives in the Codex Justinianus. Elagabalus’ cult is described by Herodian and Cassius Dio; Mithraic inscriptions to Sol Invictus Mithras are numerous.
knowAndDont.unknown: Whether Aurelian’s Sol was Roman or Syrian is debated, as is whether the 25 December festival existed before 354. The Historia Augusta is notoriously unreliable on details.

lessons.inPractice: Mark 25 December, the Dies Natalis Solis Invicti, and the winter and summer solstices in your calendar. Decide how you will keep the solstice morning: awake before dawn, a lamp lit in the dark, and the first light greeted.
reflect: What does “unconquered” mean to you? What in your life has come back after its darkest point?
How do you feel about a god whose title was claimed by emperors?
further: Steven E. Hijmans, Sol: The Sun in the Art and Religions of Rome (2009)
Michele Renee Salzman, On Roman Time: The Codex-Calendar of 354 (1990)

lessons.title: Honouring Sol today
lessons.summary: Roman polytheists and Wheel of the Year Pagans, the household Sol through the year, and how to set up his shrine.

sections.heading: Who honours him now
sections.body:
Sol is honoured today by Roman polytheists, people practising the Religio Romana or Cultus Deorum, a small reconstructed religion with groups in Italy, organisations such as Nova Roma, and many solitary practitioners. Many keep the Dies Natalis Solis Invicti on 25 December alongside or instead of Christmas, greet the dawn, and honour him on Sundays.

Modern Pagans who follow the Wheel of the Year greet the reborn sun at Yule, the winter solstice, and honour solar gods at Litha, the summer solstice. Some include Sol Invictus in their Yule rites. You will also meet the sun in astrology and planetary magic, as the planet of Sunday, success and vitality. These are related traditions, and it helps to know which you are following on a given morning.

sections.heading: Sol through the year
sections.body:
A household Sol follows the light. Every morning, a greeting at dawn, however brief. Every Sunday, a lamp and incense. At the winter solstice and 25 December, a vigil in the dark and a welcome for the returning sun. At the summer solstice, thanks at the height of the light. On 9 August, the old day of Sol Indiges, a quiet offering for the Roman sun of the Quirinal.

Sol is also honoured by living in the light: getting outside in daylight, opening curtains, keeping a regular waking time, and doing things openly rather than in secret. None of that is ancient ritual, but all of it suits the god you can see.

sections.heading: Setting up his shrine
sections.body:
Put Sol’s shrine by an east-facing window if you can, where the morning light falls on it. You need an oil lamp or a gold or yellow candle, an incense burner, a small dish for honey or fruit, and an image: a radiate head, a sun disc, a coin with Sol on it (ancient ones are affordable), or a picture of the obelisks. Bay leaves, sunflowers and golden fruit suit him. Gold and yellow are modern colours for him, and sunstone, citrine and amber modern stones.

Keep the shrine bright and clean, and let it catch the morning. A crystal or glass that throws light round the room is a pleasant modern touch.

knowAndDont.known: Modern Roman polytheist groups publish their calendars, including the Dies Natalis Solis Invicti. The Wheel of the Year’s solstice festivals are modern Pagan practice, documented by Hutton. Sunday’s name from dies Solis is certain.
knowAndDont.unknown: There is very little evidence for household worship of Sol in antiquity, beyond his image on lamps and household objects. The daily, weekly and yearly practices here are modern, built on his known festivals and character.

lessons.inPractice: Set up his shrine by an east window this week. Choose your weekly moment for him, Sunday morning or evening, and put it in your calendar.
reflect: Which window in your home catches the morning? What is there now?
What would it mean to live a little more in the light?
further: Ronald Hutton, The Stations of the Sun (1996), on midwinter and midsummer customs
Nova Roma’s published calendar and religious guides (novaroma.org)

lessons.title: Christmas, emperors and Phaethon
lessons.summary: The 25 December debate in full, the sun as a god of emperors, Phaethon’s fall, and the dangers of the sun itself.

sections.heading: Did Sol give Christmas its date?
sections.body:
The claim is everywhere: early Christians put Christmas on 25 December to take over the pagan festival of the Unconquered Sun. There is real evidence on its side. A twelfth-century note in a manuscript of the Syrian writer Dionysius bar Salibi says so, and some Christian writers of the fourth and fifth centuries played on the image of Christ as the true “Sun of Righteousness” born at the solstice.

But there is evidence the other way too. Some early Christian writers calculated Christ’s birth from the date they believed he was conceived, 25 March, which gives 25 December nine months later, without any reference to the sun festival. And there is no firm evidence that the festival of the Unconquered on 25 December is older than the calendar of 354, which also lists Christ’s birth that day. Some scholars think the pagan festival was a response to the Christian one, not the other way round. The honest answer is: nobody knows for certain.

sections.heading: The sun of emperors
sections.body:
Sol was a favourite god of emperors. Nero had himself shown with a crown of rays; a colossal bronze statue of him as the Sun stood near what became the Colosseum, which may take its name from it. Aurelian’s coins called Sol “lord of the Roman empire”, and later emperors were shown with the sun’s raised hand. The sun, alone in the sky and ruling all, was a natural image for a single ruler.

Modern devotees can honour Sol without honouring that use of him. The sun shines on everyone; Horace’s prayer asks him to see nothing greater than a city, not a man. Be wary of anyone who uses the Unconquered Sun to glorify a strong ruler or a chosen people.

sections.heading: Phaethon
sections.body:
The best-known myth of the sun in Latin literature is Greek: the story of Phaethon, told at length by Ovid at the start of Metamorphoses 2. Phaethon, son of the Sun, asks his father for proof of his parentage, and the Sun, having sworn to grant any wish, must let him drive the chariot of the sun for a day. The boy cannot control the horses; the earth burns, rivers dry, and Jupiter strikes him down with a thunderbolt to save the world. His sisters, mourning, become poplar trees weeping amber.

It is a story about power too great to handle, and a parent’s rash promise. Many devotees find it a useful warning: the sun gives life, and the same sun burns.

sections.heading: What not to do
sections.body: Never look at the sun, and never use lenses, mirrors or glass to concentrate its light. Do not sunbathe for devotion; protect your skin. Do not light candles in a sunny window and then leave them. Do not stay up all night in the cold for a solstice vigil without warm clothes and a safe place. And do not treat the sun as a sign of anyone’s superiority over anyone else: it rises on everyone.

knowAndDont.known: The Chronography of 354 lists both N Invicti and the birth of Christ on 25 December. The scholion on Dionysius bar Salibi is medieval. Ovid tells Phaethon’s story at Metamorphoses 1.750–2.400. Nero’s colossus is described by Suetonius (Nero 31) and Pliny the Elder.
knowAndDont.unknown: Which came first, the Christian feast or the pagan one on 25 December, is unresolved; see Hijmans and Thomas Talley for the two sides. Whether the Colosseum’s name comes from Nero’s colossus is likely but not certain.

lessons.inPractice: Decide how you will keep 25 December if you also keep Christmas, or if your family does: many Roman polytheists greet the sun at dawn and then join the family day. Check that you know how to protect your eyes and skin.
reflect: Does it matter to you which came first, the sun’s birthday or Christ’s? Why?
Phaethon wanted proof that he was his father’s son. What proof do you look for, and from whom?
further: Thomas J. Talley, The Origins of the Liturgical Year (1986), on the Christian date
Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.750–2.400 (public-domain translations on Project Gutenberg)

practices.title: Notice the light
practices.instructions: Through the study stage, note each day the time you first saw daylight, and one moment when the light itself caught your attention: a sunbeam, a long shadow, a bright window, the colour of the sky at evening.
practices.prompt: When did I first see the light today? When did it catch me?

stages.title: Nine dawns
stages.intro: Nine mornings of greeting the sun as it rises. If sunrise is impossibly early or late for you this season, greet the first daylight you see, or the sunset. Nine-day periods were used in Roman religion for other rites; here nine frames a practice, not a claim about ancient custom.

practices.title: Greeting the sun
practices.instructions:
Each morning, at or near sunrise: wash your hands and face and cover your head. Give a word or a grain of incense to Janus, opener of the day. Light the lamp, face east with your eyes lowered, raise your right hand, and say Horace’s prayer or your own: “Life-giving Sun, who bring out the day and hide it, born another and the same: be honoured.” Name one thing you will do in the light today, openly and well. Stand in the light for a minute. Name Vesta last, turn to your right, uncover, and put out the lamp.

If cloud hides the sun, greet him anyway. He is there.
practices.prompt: What did the sky do this morning? What did I promise to do in the light, and did I do it?

practices.title: A sunset watched to the end
practices.instructions: Once in the nine days, watch a sunset from start to finish, from somewhere with a clear western view, without your phone. When the light is gone, say: “Sol, who hide the day, be honoured. Rise again.”
practices.prompt: What did I feel as the light went? What did the dark feel like after?

stages.title: Before the solstice
stages.intro: A few days to stop and decide. Sol asks for daily attention more than great ritual, and a dedication to him is a promise to keep greeting the light and living openly in it. Stopping, pausing, or choosing another god or path is a good outcome.

practices.title: Write it out in daylight
practices.instructions: Answer the questions below in your journal, a few each day, sitting in daylight if you can. Read back your notes from the nine dawns first.
practices.prompt: What am I drawn to here: the god, the dawn practice, the solstice festivals, or the idea of being unconquered?

questions: Did the nine dawns feel like devotion, or like a struggle with my alarm clock? Either answer is useful.
Can I keep a daily or weekly greeting, and the solstice and 25 December, for a year?
Am I comfortable with the Roman forms of prayer, and with the honest uncertainty about his midwinter birthday?
How do I feel about Sol as a god of emperors, and can I honour him without that?
Am I drawn to Sol himself, or to Apollo, Janus, or the sun of the Wheel of the Year, who might fit better?
Would I rather keep greeting the dawn without dedicating? That is a perfectly good choice.

stages.title: The dedication at sunrise
stages.intro: If you have decided to go ahead, hold this at sunrise, ideally on 25 December, the Dies Natalis Solis Invicti, on the winter or summer solstice, or on a Sunday. Begin in the dark and finish in the light. It is a self-dedication, not an initiation; it does not make you a pontiff of Sol or a Mithraic initiate. You are dedicating yourself as a devotee who greets the light and keeps his days.

rite.title: Self-dedication to Sol
rite.summary: A lamp lit before dawn, hands washed and head covered, Janus first, Horace’s prayer as the light comes, a spoken dedication, incense, honey and golden fruit, a raised right hand, and Vesta last.

ingredients.name: A bowl of clean water and a towel
Clean clothes, white or gold if you have them
A new gold candle or a filled oil lamp
Honey and a golden fruit (an orange, apricot or golden apple) on a dish
A cup of wine or juice
A sunstone or piece of amber for the shrine

rite.preparation: Check the exact time of sunrise. The night before, set everything out by your east window. Write your dedication: who you are, that you dedicate yourself to Sol as a devotee, for how long (a year is wise), and what you will do: greet the dawn (daily or on Sundays), keep 25 December and the solstices, and live and act openly. Read it aloud until it flows. Set an alarm for half an hour before sunrise.

steps.title: Light in the dark
steps.instructions: While it is still dark, wash your hands and face, dress and cover your head. Light the lamp. Sit with it for a few minutes in the dark, waiting.

steps.title: Janus first
steps.instructions: Give a few grains of incense to Janus, opener of the day.
steps.spoken:
Father Janus, first in every prayer,
open the door of the day, and the way to Sol.

steps.title: As the light comes
steps.instructions: When the sky begins to brighten, stand and face east with your eyes lowered. Raise your right hand, palm out. Add incense.
steps.spoken:
Alme Sol, life-giving Sun,
who with your shining chariot bring out the day and hide it,
and are born another and the same,
Unconquered, lord of the light,
or by whatever name it is right to call you:
I offer you this incense, and I pray good prayers,
that you may be willing and favourable
to me, my house and my household.

steps.title: Read the dedication
steps.instructions: Read your dedication aloud, clearly and in full. If you stumble, stop and begin it again from the start.

steps.title: Offer
steps.instructions: Set the honey and fruit before the lamp, with the bay leaves around them. Pour a little wine or juice into the dish.
steps.spoken:
Sol, be honoured by this honey, this fruit and this wine.
As I have spoken, so I will do.

steps.title: Stand in the light
steps.instructions: Stand in the growing light, eyes on the land or the sky, never on the sun. Let it reach your face.

steps.title: Vesta last, and turn
steps.instructions: Name Vesta, turn to your right, uncover your head, and put out the lamp.
steps.spoken: Vesta, keeper of the hearth, be honoured. The sun is risen. It is done.

rite.closing: Eat some of the fruit yourself for breakfast, and share it if you can. Leave the god’s portion on the shrine until sunset, then return it to the earth or compost. Keep your dedication on the shrine where the morning light reaches it. Note the date for your rededication, or keep it each 25 December.
rite.safety: Never look directly at the sun. Never leave the lamp or incense unattended. If you hold the rite outdoors in winter, dress warmly and stay somewhere safe and lit. Grapes, raisins and wine are toxic to dogs and cats; keep the dish out of reach. Keep honey from babies under a year old.

stages.title: Born another and the same
stages.intro: Sol’s ongoing worship follows the light: a greeting at dawn, a weekly lamp on Sunday, the solstices and 25 December through the year, and a rededication when the sun turns.

practices.title: Sunday lamp
practices.instructions: Each Sunday, dies Solis, greet the sun at or after dawn with incense, a lamp and Horace’s prayer, and name one thing you did openly and well that week. Greet him on other mornings too, as often as you can.
practices.prompt: What did I do in the light this week?

practices.title: The turning year
practices.instructions: Keep the winter solstice with a vigil and a lamp lit in the dark, and 25 December, the Dies Natalis Solis Invicti, with a greeting at dawn, incense, golden fruit and, if you like, a game or race in memory of the thirty races in the Circus. Keep the summer solstice with thanks at the height of the light, and 9 August for Sol Indiges. Rededicate on 25 December, reading your dedication and saying honestly how you kept it.
practices.prompt: What came back to me this year after a dark time?
